transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-10-12 16:32 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Ravi (CTO - HyperDocs), Sofia (Eng Manager - HyperDocs), Liam (Security Lead - HyperDocs)

Summary: quick scoping on POC success criteria, workload sizing and timeline; decision criteria for hosted vs dedicated vs private

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining, we're Maya from Redwood, and Diego our solutions engineer is here as well, how's everyone doin?
[00:08] Ravi: good thanks, thx for the time, we wanted to get clarity on what a POC would look like and which deployment mode makes sense for our use case, which is an in-editor AI suggestion flow with real-time latency needs.
[00:22] Maya: perfect, can you give us the high level success criteria for the POC? like SLOs, cost thresh, timeline?
[00:28] Sofia: sure, success is two fold: latency under 200ms 95th for single-turn suggestions, and cost per 1k requests under our threshold, plus no PII leaving our control, so encryption and audit logs are important.
[00:41] Diego: ok noted, 200ms 95th is ambitious for a hosted multi-tenant path but doable with right model selection and batching config; also sequence length and prompt size matter — what's your avg token length?
[00:52] Ravi: typical request is 40-60 tokens, worst case around 200 tokens for longer context. QPS depends on gradual rollout, initial 50 qps then scale to 300 qps in steady state.
[01:05] Maya: great, that gives us a sizing target. For deployment modes, quick run through: Hosted = fastest to start, managed, usage pricing; Dedicated = reserved GPU pools for predictability and throughput; Private = VPC/on-prem for strict compliance and data residency.
[01:22] Liam: on private, we have a couple customers with data residency plus KMS requirements; we might need a private option if SOC2 plus regional residency is required.
[01:31] Diego: totally, private gives you customer-managed KMS and no egress from your VPC to our multi-tenant plane, but it adds setup time, infra ops and an enterprise contract.
[01:42] Sofia: timeline wise how long for each?
[01:45] Maya: Hosted — you can be started in days, dedicated — a few weeks for capacity reservation and tuning, private — multiple weeks to months depending on network and approvals.
[01:56] Ravi: we have procurement constraints, but if hosted can meet our SLO and data handling with signed DPA, we'd prefer to start there and only move to dedicated if costs or latency are problematic.
[02:08] Diego: makes sense as a strategy. For the POC we propose a two-phase approach: Phase 1 hosted pilot with realistic traffic replay and latency/cost measurement; Phase 2 if needed run a dedicated bench to compare unit economics and tail latency.
[02:21] Maya: for benchmarks we'll need sample traffic, target sequences, error budget and any auth flows; Diego will propose specific benchmark configs.
[02:30] Diego: yes I'll prepare a benchmark plan — model variants (gpt-like open models), tokenization, batching settings, KV cache behavior simulation, and quantization profiles. We'll measure p50/p95/p99, throughput (qps), and cost per 1k tokens.
[02:47] Sofia: small note — we use per-request session state; KV cache behavior matters because we sometimes reuse context across keystrokes. If cache hits are high that can change batching and throughput.
[02:59] Diego: good point, we'll include prefix/KV cache warmup cases. Also we'll log memory/kv hit rates.
[03:08] Liam: security — SOC2 is baseline; we need audit logs, SSO/SAML, RBAC, and customer-managed KMS for private. Also data retention settings. Can you share security docs?
[03:20] Maya: yes we'll send the security pack link, includes SOC2 attestation, encryption in transit + at rest details, and KMS integration notes. For hosted we offer encrypted storage and restricted retention settings; for private you host keys.
[03:33] Ravi: great. Competitors — we looked at Anthropic and some in-house infra; main differentiator is cost predictability and easier rollouts.
[03:43] Diego: in-house infra gives control but large ops overhead; Redwood can run hosted then transition to dedicated if predictability is needed. We can also do a canary/dry run to emulate peak.
[03:55] Sofia: about metrics — we need token-level cost breakdown and per-route dashboards during the POC, is that available?
[04:02] Maya: yes our console provides token cost breakdown, per-route latency, and tracing hooks. We'll enable a short retention window for the POC.
[04:10] Ravi: timeline: we want a bench week of 2026-10-19, does that work?
[04:14] Diego: yes Diego: we can target that, pending sample traffic and access.
[04:18] Maya: recap — Redwood to send POC scope + pricing, SE to send benchmark config, customer to send sample traffic + SLOs, security to exchange docs. We'll schedule the benchmark week of 10-19.
[04:31] Liam: one question on cost: how do you surface the difference between batching gains and quality regressions from quantization?
[04:38] Diego: we'll capture quality via prompt-based evals and compare outputs across quantized/different kernels; batching shouldn't change generation semantics but in practice we measure output diffs on a holdout set. We'll include that in the POC acceptance criteria.
[04:54] Sofia: accepted — we want both perf and quality gates.
[04:58] Maya: ok thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the scope doc and schedule.
[05:03] Ravi: thanks all, look forward to the benchmark.

End of call.

Notes on transcript quality: some words mistranscribed (k v cache sometimes appears as "K V cash"), and speaker labels occasionally abbreviated.
